Thursday evening, after the B2 class. The day before, Ecaterina spoke to Andrés for the first time in forty years, by video call, with Marta’s help. Ana and Domnul Dan want to hear everything.
Tell us, please. What did he say to you?
At first, nothing. He looked at me for a long time. Marta had warned me that sometimes he didn’t recognise anyone.
He asked me who I was. I told him my name. Then he put on his glasses and asked me if I was still translating.
Was that the first thing he asked you?
Yes. I answered that I had stopped translating, but that I had just started again. And that I was translating his granddaughter’s novel.
He laughed. He told me he had always known I would come back to that book one way or another. And he assured me he still had my Cortázar on his bedside table.
Did he talk to you about 1987?
No. I tried to apologise, but he interrupted me. He told me there was no need, that on that day he had been afraid too.
At the end he asked me to go to Madrid. He begged me not to wait any longer, to go before he forgot my face. And he added that this time he wouldn’t let me leave without saying goodbye.
(takes a plane ticket out of her bag) That we would see each other on 8 December. I booked it last night. Andrei showed me how to book it online.

In reported speech, the reporting verb is stressed and “que” links up with the next word: «me di-JO-que-ve-NÍ-a».
-ara / -iera, stressed on the second-to-last syllable: vi-NIE-ra, fue-ra, es-pe-RA-ra.
Stress on the first syllable (esdrújula): VÍS-pe-ra.
1. The tense shift in reported speech
When the reporting verb is in the past (dijo, preguntó, contestó), the tenses “move back”:
que había tenido miedo (pluperfect) / que tuvo miedo
If the reporting verb is in the present («dice que…») or the information is still true, the tenses don’t change: «Me dijo que tiene ochenta y nueve años» (he still is).
Me pidió que fuera a Madrid.
Me rogó que no esperara más.
Yes/no questions are introduced with “si” (if), WITHOUT “que”: «Me preguntó si seguía…», not «Me preguntó que si…» (informal; avoid it in writing).
ir / llevar (if the place has changed)
The person changes too: «Tengo TU Cortázar» → «Me dijo que tenía MI Cortázar».
He assured me he had it.
He warned me he didn’t always recognise people.
He begged me not to wait any longer.
He confessed that he had been afraid too.
He admitted he had been wrong.

Verbs of influence (pedir, rogar, aconsejar, ordenar, prohibir) take the subjunctive. Verbs of communication (decir, asegurar, contar) take the indicative, but “decir” can take the subjunctive when it passes on an order: «Me dijo que viniera» (told me to come) versus «Me dijo que venía» (told me he was coming).
He begged me not to wait any longer.
He assured me he still had my book.

¿Qué fue lo primero que le preguntó Andrés?
An excerpt from a newspaper article reporting an interview with Marta Gil. Notice the reporting verbs.
Marta Gil welcomes us into the small flat in the Barrio de las Letras where she lives with her grandfather. She warns us from the start that she won’t talk about her family’s private life.
We ask her how the novel came about. She explains that she started writing it three years ago, when her grandfather asked her to write down his memories before it was too late.
She admits that at first she didn’t know whether that love story was real or invented. “My grandfather assured me it was all true, but I thought he was exaggerating,” she confesses with a smile.
At the end of the interview, we ask her whether the heroine exists. Marta is silent for a few seconds. Then she says she will meet her very soon, on 8 December, in Madrid.
De la vida privada de su familia

The video call was arranged for Wednesday at seven in the evening, Bucharest time, six in Madrid. Marta had explained by message that her grandfather was better in the afternoons, after his siesta, and that in the mornings he was usually confused. She had also warned that she couldn’t promise anything: there were days when Andrés called her Pilar, like her mother, and days when he didn’t know where he was.

Ecaterina asked to make the call from Ana and Mihai’s house. She said there were too many memories in her flat and that she needed a place with children, noise and the smell of cooking. Elena, who had heard all about it, made sarmale. Rosa Elena drew a picture for the gentleman in Madrid: a huge tree with lots of books hanging from its branches like fruit.

Ecaterina arrived half an hour early, in a dark blue dress nobody had ever seen her wear, and with lipstick on. Ana said nothing to her, but Mihai whispered in her ear that she looked like a bride. Ecaterina heard him, because her hearing was much better than her eyesight, and told him that if he kept talking nonsense she would correct all his verbs for the week.

While they waited, Ecaterina sat on the sofa with her hands on her knees, very upright, like a pupil before an exam. She asked Ana what she should say first. Ana answered that she didn’t know, that perhaps there was no need to prepare anything. Ecaterina confessed that for a week she had been writing sentences in a notebook and crossing them all out. She showed her the notebook: it had twelve pages full of crossed-out sentences, in Romanian and Spanish. At the end of the last page, not crossed out, there was just one word: “Hola”.

At seven o’clock sharp, Marta’s face appeared on the computer screen in the living room. She was younger and prettier than in the photos. She greeted everyone, smiled nervously and said her grandfather was beside her, but that first she wanted to let them know he was a bit tired that day. Then she turned the camera.

Andrés was sitting in an armchair by a window, with a blanket over his legs. He was very thin and his hair was completely white, but he wore the same round glasses, or very similar ones. He looked at the screen without expression for a time that seemed endless to everyone. Nobody in the living room in Bucharest dared to breathe. Even Rosa Elena kept still.

Then Andrés asked, in a weak but clear voice, who that lady was. Marta told him, very slowly, that it was Ecaterina, from Bucharest. Andrés repeated the name twice, as if he were trying it out in his mouth. Then he asked his granddaughter to give him his reading glasses, although he was already wearing them. Marta took them off and put them back on him. And then something changed in his face.

Ecaterina said afterwards that at that moment she felt the ground disappear beneath her feet. He didn’t ask her why she had left, or where she had been for forty years, or whether she had married. He asked her if she was still translating. It was exactly what he used to ask her every evening, in the back room of the bookshop, when she came in from the office with a book under her arm.

She answered that she had stopped translating ten years before, but had just started again. She explained that she was translating Marta’s novel. Andrés laughed, a short, hoarse laugh, and said he had always known she would come back to that book one way or another. Then he assured her he still had her Cortázar, the one she had left in the bookshop in 1987, on his bedside table.

Ecaterina then tried to say what she had been preparing for forty years. She began to apologise for leaving without saying goodbye. Andrés interrupted her with a wave of his hand. He told her there was no need. He confessed that on that autumn day he had been afraid too; that he had seen the light on in the window of her flat at three in the morning and hadn’t dared to go up.

In the living room in Bucharest, Elena was wiping her eyes with her apron. Mihai was squeezing Ana’s hand under the table. Costel, who was connected from his lorry cab in a car park in Hungary, had switched off his microphone so that nobody could hear him crying, but everyone could see in his little window on the screen how he wiped his face with his shirt sleeve.

They talked for twenty minutes. Sometimes Andrés lost the thread and stared out of the window. Then Marta would quietly remind him who he was talking to, and he would come back. At one of those moments, he asked Ecaterina whether she still liked the hot chocolate with churros at the Plaza de San Ginés. She answered that she hadn’t tasted it since. He told her that was a crime and she had to put it right.

Towards the end, Andrés’s voice grew weaker. Marta told them her grandfather was getting tired and they would have to finish soon. Then Andrés leant towards the camera, so far that his face filled the whole screen, and asked Ecaterina to come to Madrid. He begged her not to wait any longer, to come before he forgot her face. And he added, with a smile, that this time he wouldn’t let her leave without saying goodbye.

Ecaterina promised him she would come. She didn’t say when, because she didn’t know yet. Andrés nodded, closed his eyes and fell asleep in the armchair, suddenly, the way children fall asleep. Marta thanked everyone, her voice breaking, and switched off the camera. The screen went black. In the living room in Bucharest, nobody said anything for a long minute.

Costel switched his microphone back on. From his cab in Hungary, his voice still shaky, he said he had to confess something: that during the call a Hungarian lorry driver had knocked on his window to ask if he was all right, and he had told him yes, he was just watching a love film. He added that the Hungarian had asked to watch it too, and was at that moment sitting next to him in the cab, blowing his nose.

It was Rosa Elena who broke the silence. She went up to Ecaterina with her drawing of the book tree, put it on her knees and asked her if the gentleman in Madrid was her boyfriend. Ecaterina laughed for the first time all evening. She told her yes, he had been, a long time ago, when she was young and he still had all his hair black.
“And why didn’t you marry him?” asked Rosa Elena, with the relentless logic of children.

Ecaterina took a while to answer. Then she told her that sometimes grown-ups are afraid of things children aren’t afraid of, and that’s why children are braver. Rosa Elena thought for a moment and advised her, very seriously, to go and see him soon, before he got any older. Everyone burst out laughing, including Ecaterina, who promised she would take her advice.

When everyone had left, Ana walked Ecaterina to the taxi. At the door, the old lady stopped and told her something Ana would never forget. She said that for forty years she had thought her life had broken in two on that autumn day, and that the good half had stayed in Madrid. But that this evening, in a living room full of children and the smell of sarmale, she had understood she was wrong: the good half had been here too, in Bucharest, all along.

That same night, back at home, Ecaterina called Andrei and asked him to come and help her with the computer. Andrei arrived at ten, by bike, his hair wet from the rain. Ecaterina explained that she wanted to buy a plane ticket to Madrid online and had no idea how to do it. Andrei asked her for when. She answered as soon as possible, but that she didn’t want to go alone.

Andrei called Ana from Ecaterina’s kitchen at half past ten and asked if she would be free over the December long weekend. Ana replied that she would have to ask Mihai. Mihai, who was beside her and had heard everything, took the phone and told Andrei that Ana would be free, that he would stay with Rosa Elena and that, while she was at it, she should bring him back a good chorizo from Madrid.

And so it was that at a quarter past eleven at night, an eighty-year-old translator bought two plane tickets online for the first time in her life: Bucharest–Madrid, 8 December, in the names of Ecaterina Ionescu and Ana García. Andrei showed her how to print the boarding pass. Ecaterina put it in her bag, inside the yellowed envelope, next to the letter she had never managed to post.
Before going to bed, she sent Marta a message with only one spelling mistake: “Tell your grandfather I’m coming on 8 December. To keep the Cortázar for me. And that this time I will say goodbye.”

“perder el hilo” = to lose the thread
“se hiciera más mayor” = got older (imperfect subjunctive)
